title: Building a Course
text:
Why a template?
Building an online course should be about your subject, not about web design.

The template gives you:

Chapters, navigation and search
Quizzes with instant feedback
The university’s corporate design, already applied

title: Building a Course
text:
The whole workflow

Plan on paper: outcomes first
Write each chapter as a text file
Render with one click in RStudio
Check with the checklist
Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages


Mention that steps 2 to 4 repeat many times. Publishing is the routine render, commit, push.

title: Building a Course
text:
Plan from the outcome


Not this
“Understand hand hygiene”

This
“List the five moments for hand disinfection”

title: Building a Course
text:
One chapter, one rhythm

Objectives
Short sections, each with its own heading
One key point
Two to four questions


Questions are part of the teaching, not an extra.

title: Building a Course with This Template
text:
You know your subject and you want to teach it online. What you do not want is to learn web design, or to argue with a learning platform’s editor about where a picture goes.
This template turns plain text files into a complete course website: chapters with a sidebar, search, self-check quizzes, lecture slides, a dark mode, and a layout that works on a phone. Colours, typeface and logo placement already follow the Universitätsmedizin Göttingen corporate design, so nobody has to decide them again.
This course is built with the template it teaches. Every feature you read about is in use on the page in front of you, and the files behind these pages are the worked examples. When a chapter says “see how it is done”, open the matching .qmd file and look.

    B --> C["Step 3<br/>Check the pages<br/>in the docs folder"]
    C --> D["Step 4<br/>Publish on GitHub<br/>or GitLab Pages"]

Figure 1: The workflow of this course. You repeat the first three steps as often as you like; publishing is a routine of three clicks.

title: Building a Course with This Template
text:
How this course works
There are eight short chapters, in four groups. Each has the same shape: objectives at the top, explanation with examples, and questions at the end. Plan on about three to four hours in total, and take them in order the first time. You can stop after any chapter and come back.






flowchart LR

        A["1 Set up<br/>and first render"] --> B["2 Plan and<br/>structure"]
    end
    subgraph G2["Write"]
        C["3 Write<br/>text"] --> D["4 Images, tables,<br/>references"] --> E["5 Quizzes"]
    end
    subgraph G3["Slides and release"]
        F["6 Slides"] --> G["7 Check before<br/>release"] --> H["8 Publish"]
    end
    B --> C
    E --> F

    classDef writing fill:#134a84,stroke:#134a84,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff
    classDef finish fill:#f1a400,stroke:#f1a400,stroke-width:2px,color:#000000
    class A,B basics
    class C,D,E writing
    class F,G,H finish




Figure 2: Route through the material. Take the chapters in order the first time.





If you are in a hurry: Chapter 1 gets you a running project, Chapter 7 is the checklist, and Chapter 8 gets the course online. Everything in between is what makes the course good.
crumbs: Building a Course with This Template

title: Building a Course with This Template
text:
Try it now
Every chapter ends with questions like this one. Choose an answer and press Check answer; the page tells you whether you were right and why. Nothing is recorded anywhere, so guessing costs you nothing.

In this template, what does one chapter correspond to?

One line in the navigation file
One .qmd text file
One folder of images
One page in the Word document you started from


Each chapter is a single .qmd file: plain text with a small amount of markup. The navigation file only lists the chapters and puts them in order. Chapter 2 covers how the two fit together.


Some questions ask for a word instead. The tool that turns the text files into a website is called ? (type it in and click elsewhere).
crumbs: Building a Course with This Template

title: Building a Course with This Template
text:
Before you start






What you need



R and RStudio, both free. RStudio includes Quarto, the tool that builds the website, so there is nothing else to install. You will not write or run any R code: R is simply what RStudio runs on. A modern web browser is all a reader needs.








Using this as your starting point



Chapter 1 explains exactly how to copy this project and turn it into your own course. In short: duplicate the folder, replace the chapters, change a handful of lines in one settings file.
crumbs: Building a Course with This Template

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
In this chapter

Explain what publishing means here, and what only has to be done once
Prepare the project for publishing
Put the course online and update it later
Check the published course, and fix what went wrong
Know what “public” means before you press the button
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
1 What publishing means
When you press Render Website, RStudio builds the course into a folder called docs. That folder is a complete website. Publishing means copying that folder to a place on the internet that shows it as a web page.
GitHub and GitLab are websites where projects are stored online. Both can also show the website files they hold to the public: this feature is called Pages, and the result is an ordinary web address. Your course is a set of files; the platform hands them to whoever asks.
Three words you will meet:

Repository: your project folder, stored online together with its history.
Commit: saving a labelled snapshot of your changes. You give it a short message, such as “Update chapter 3”.
Push: sending your saved snapshots from your computer to the online repository.


Key point
The routine every time is three steps: render, commit, push. The rest of this chapter is a one-off setup, and it is fine, even normal, to have someone from your team do that part with you.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
2 Who does what



Table 1: The one-off setup and the routine












What
How often
Who




A
Create the online repository, connect it to your computer, switch on Pages
Once per course
You with help, or your team


B
Render, commit, push
Every release
You






If your team has already set up the repository and Pages for you, skip to the routine.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
3 GitHub or GitLab?
Your institution decides; you do not need to choose. Both do the job.



Table 2: GitHub and GitLab Pages compared











GitHub
GitLab




Address of the course
https://<account>.github.io/<repository>/
Depends on the installation, for example https://<group>.pages.<institution>/<project>/


Who can read it
Anyone, on the free plan
Anyone, or only members of the project, if the installation allows


Setup
A settings page, no extra files
Needs a small automation file; see below






If your course must not be public (for example, only for enrolled students), do not use a free public GitHub repository. Ask your team about the options on your institution’s GitLab, or about linking the course from the learning platform behind a login.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
4 Before you publish

Finish Chapter 7: the checklist.
In _quarto.yml, set site-url to the address the course will have (from the table above). If you do not know it yet, publish once, read the address off the Pages settings, and then correct it.
Click Render Website one last time.

The project contains an empty file named .nojekyll. Leave it alone; it tells GitHub to serve your files exactly as they are. It starts with a dot, so your computer may hide it. That is fine.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
5 One-off setup

Step A1: an online repository

GitHubGitLab


The simplest route for a beginner is the free program GitHub Desktop.

Create an account at github.com if you do not have one. Install GitHub Desktop from desktop.github.com and sign in.
In GitHub Desktop, choose File → Add local repository… and pick your project folder. If it says that the folder is not a repository yet, click the link offering to create one.
Click Publish repository. Give it a name in lowercase with hyphens. For free Pages the repository has to be public, so untick “Keep this code private”. Click Publish.



GitLab installations differ (most institutions log in with the university account), and there is no official desktop program. Ask your team to create the project and to connect it to RStudio with you. Once that is done, RStudio’s Git tab (in the upper-right panel) does everything in the routine below.





Step A2: switch on Pages

GitHubGitLab



Open the repository on github.com and click Settings.
In the left menu, click Pages.
Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch.
Under Branch, choose main and, in the folder drop-down next to it, /docs. Click Save.
Wait a minute or two and reload the page. The address of your course appears at the top.



GitLab shows Pages through a small automation file in the project, called .gitlab-ci.yml. It differs between installations, so the template does not include one. Ask whoever administers your GitLab; they will know the standard one for your institution and can add it in a few minutes. Afterwards you never touch it.






For the person who sets it up





A minimal file that publishes the already-built docs folder, as a starting point; adapt it to your installation’s runners and rules:
pages:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - mkdir -p public
    - cp -r docs/. public/
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - public
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
It does not build the course. The author builds it in RStudio and commits the docs folder.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
6 The routine: render, commit, push
Every time you want to release a new version:

Render. In RStudio, click Render Website and wait for it to finish without errors.
Commit and push. Save a snapshot and send it online. Steps below.
Wait, then look. It takes from a few seconds to a few minutes for the change to appear. Then open your course address and press Ctrl+F5 so the browser fetches the newest version.

Committing and pushing, in detail:

GitHub DesktopRStudio Git tab


Open GitHub Desktop. The left panel lists the changed files. There are usually many, because the whole website is rebuilt; that is normal. In the box at the bottom left, type a short summary such as Update chapter 3, and click Commit to main. Then click Push origin at the top.


Open the Git tab. Click one file, press Ctrl+A to select all, and click Stage. Click Commit, type a message, and click Commit again. Then click the green Push arrow.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
7 Check the published course
Open the live address and try it like a learner would:

The navigation, sidebar and logo appear, and the colours are right.
Pictures load, and a diagram is drawn.
A quiz question works when you click Check answer.
Search finds a word from a chapter.
The Slides link in the top menu opens the slides.
It looks right on your phone.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
8 When something goes wrong



Table 3: Publishing problems and their usual fixes










What you see
Likely cause
What to do




“404” or “Site not found” on the address
Pages is not switched on yet, or points at the wrong folder
Check Settings → Pages: branch main, folder /docs. Wait a few minutes after saving


The page shows but with no styling, or pictures are missing
Only some files were pushed, or .nojekyll is missing
In GitHub Desktop check that no files are left uncommitted; check that docs/.nojekyll exists and re-render


An old version is displayed
The browser cached it, or the push did not happen
Press Ctrl+F5; check that GitHub Desktop says nothing is waiting to push


Your change is not there at all
You edited but did not render, or rendered but did not commit
Repeat render, commit, push, in that order


A chapter you removed still shows up
It was not cleared from docs
Use Render Website (the whole site), then commit and push again


A page works on the site but not in a link from your platform
The link uses the wrong address
Use the address shown in Pages settings, with https://
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
9 Fixing mistakes
Publishing is not a one-way street. If you find an error, fix the text file, render, commit and push again; the corrected version replaces the old one. The repository keeps every earlier version too, so a change can be rolled back with help from someone technical.
To take the course offline, ask your team. On GitHub, making the repository private or deleting it removes the site, and on GitLab the administrator can switch Pages off.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
10 Public means public






Read this before the first push




Everyone can read it. A public course is visible to the whole internet, including search engines.
Not just the finished pages: the source too. The repository contains your chapter files, drafts and images, and their whole history.
Deleting is not enough. If something confidential or personal is committed and you delete it a day later, it is still in the history. If this happens, tell your team at once and do not try to hide it yourself.
Quiz answers are readable by anyone who looks at the page source. Never put an exam behind these quizzes.
Never commit patient data, passwords, access tokens or unpublished results.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
11 Your course is live
That is the whole workflow: plan on paper, write in text files, render, check, commit, push. The first course takes the longest. The second takes a fraction of the time, because you now know where everything is. Copy this project again for your next one.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages
text:
12 Check your understanding




Which folder contains the finished website that gets published?

images
assets
docs
slides


Render Website writes the finished course into docs. That folder is what GitHub Pages serves. You never edit it by hand.



You have corrected a typo in a chapter, but the live site still shows the old text an hour later. What is the most likely reason?

GitHub is slow today
You edited the file but did not render, commit and push
The typo is cached in the file .nojekyll
The chapter is too long


A change only reaches the live site after all three steps. The most common cause of “nothing happened” is one that was skipped. After a push, a few minutes’ wait and Ctrl+F5 cover the rest.



You accidentally committed a spreadsheet with patient names, then deleted it in the next commit. What should you do?

Nothing; it is deleted now
Delete the repository’s Pages setting
Tell your team and your data-protection contact straight away
Rename the spreadsheet


The file is still in the repository’s history, and if the repository is public it may already have been seen or copied. It needs to be dealt with by people who can remove it properly, and quickly.


The three steps of the routine are render, commit, and ?.
crumbs: Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages

title: Slides
text:
In this chapter

Decide whether a course needs slides at all
Open, edit and preview the slide deck that comes with the template
Structure slides, add speaker notes and reveal content step by step
Create a second deck, and link to it
Export slides as a PDF

title: Slides
text:
1 Do you need slides?
Not every course does. The chapters are meant to be read on their own. Slides are for a different situation: you presenting live, in a lecture or a webinar, where learners need something to look at while you talk.
If you would only be copying the chapter text onto slides, skip them.

title: Slides
section: 2 The deck that comes with the template
text:
2 The deck that comes with the template
Open slides/lecture-01.qmd. It is a text file like a chapter, and it turns into a full-screen presentation. It has the university’s logo top right and the blue rule under each slide title, so it matches the course.
To see it, render the website as usual and click Slides in the top menu. The deck opens in a new tab, and a click anywhere then the arrow keys move through it.






Useful keys while presenting



Arrow keys move between slides, F goes full-screen, S opens the speaker view with your notes and a timer, O shows an overview of all slides, and Esc leaves the overview.

title: Slides
text:
3 Structure
The top of the file, between the two lines of dashes, has the title and settings. Leave the settings as they are and change only title, subtitle and author. Below it, every ## heading starts a new slide:
## The problem

Learners forget most of what they hear once.

## Our approach

- Explain briefly
- Let them try
- Ask a question
Compare with a chapter: the same headings and lists, only shorter. A slide should hold one idea and no more than about six lines.

Reveal step by step
To show content one piece at a time, put a line containing . . . (three dots separated by spaces) where the pause should be:
## Question

What is the first step?

. . .

**Render the website.**


Speaker notes
Notes are visible to you only, in the speaker view (S):
## Our approach

- Explain briefly
- Let them try

::: {.notes}
Mention the example from last week here. Two minutes.
:::


Two columns, images, emphasis
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Text on the left.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Caption](../images/placeholder.svg)
:::
::::
Notice the ../ before images. The slides live one folder deeper than the chapters, so they have to step up out of it to find the pictures.
Two coloured boxes are ready-made for emphasis: ::: {.callout-blue} (white text on blue) and ::: {.callout-yellow} (black text on yellow), both used as a normal block with a closing :::. Use them sparingly.

title: Slides
text:
4 Slides that work

One idea per slide. If you need “and” in the heading, make two slides.
Few words, large. If it cannot be read from the back of the room, cut it.
Do not read the slide aloud. Put the detail in the chapter and the point on the slide.
Use pictures for what a picture shows better than words, with alt text as in Chapter 4.
End with what to do, not with “Thank you” or “Questions?”.

title: Slides
text:
5 A second deck

In the Files panel, open the slides folder. Copy lecture-01.qmd and name the copy lecture-02.qmd.
Change its title and slides, and render the website.
Link to it from where learners will look for it: from a chapter with [Lecture 2](slides/lecture-02.qmd), or (from within the slides folder itself) simply lecture-02.qmd. You can also add it to the top menu in _quarto.yml, under navbar:, in the same way as the existing Slides entry.

title: Slides
text:
6 A PDF for handouts
Open the slides in the browser and add ?print-pdf to the end of the address, so it ends in lecture-01.html?print-pdf. Press Enter, then use the browser’s print function and choose Save as PDF. In the print dialog, set Margins to None and tick Background graphics. The PDF then keeps the colours and the logo.

title: Slides
text:
7 Check your understanding




What starts a new slide?

A blank line
A line with three dashes only
A ## heading
The words “Next slide”


Every second-level heading starts a new slide, exactly as it starts a new section in a chapter.



A slide has ten bullet points in small print. What is the best repair?

Reduce the font size further
Split it into several slides with one idea each, and move the detail into the chapter
Put the bullets into a table
Make the text yellow


A slide supports the speaker; it is not a document. Cut it down and let the chapter carry the detail.



You want a picture on a slide. The file is images/diagram.png in the project. What is the link in the slide file?

images/diagram.png
../images/diagram.png
/images/diagram.png
diagram.png


The slide files live in the slides folder, one level below the project’s main folder, so they must step up with ../ to reach the images.


To show a slide’s content one piece at a time, you put a line with the characters ? at the point of the pause. (Type them with spaces.)

title: Images, Tables, Diagrams and References
text:
In this chapter

Add an image with a caption and a text alternative, and refer to it in the text
Build a table and keep it readable
Draw a simple diagram without a drawing program
Embed a video responsibly
Cite a source and get the reference list for free

title: Images, Tables, Diagrams and References
text:
1 Images
Put every image file in the images/ folder. Then insert it in one of two ways.

Visual mode: Insert → Figure / Image…, pick the file, type a caption and the Alt text, and confirm.
Source mode:

![A short caption under the picture](images/placeholder.svg){#fig-demo fig-alt="A dark blue placeholder picture with the words: Your picture goes here."}
Here is the result. Click the picture: it opens enlarged, which helps with screenshots and detailed diagrams.






Figure 1: A short caption under the picture




Alt text is not optional
The alt text is a description of the picture for people who cannot see it: blind and low-vision learners using a screen reader, and anyone whose image has not loaded. In the EU, accessibility is also a legal requirement for most public-sector websites. Write what the picture shows and why it is there, in a sentence or two: “Screenshot of the Build tab with the Render Website button highlighted”, not “screenshot” or “image1”.
The caption and the alt text do different jobs. The caption is for everybody and says what to notice. The alt text stands in for the picture.


Referring to a picture
Notice the {#fig-demo} in the source above. That label lets you point to the figure by number from anywhere in the chapter: typing @fig-demo produces Figure 1. The number updates itself if you add a figure before it. Labels for figures must start with fig-, and for tables with tbl-.


Choosing and preparing images



Table 1: Which file type to use





Situation
Best format




Screenshot, diagram, chart
PNG, or SVG for drawings


Photograph
JPG


Logo or line drawing you can scale
SVG







Keep files small. A photo straight from a phone can be many megabytes and makes the course slow to load. Scale it down (a width of about 1600 pixels is plenty) before adding it.
Do not put text in images. It cannot be searched, resized or read aloud. Put the text in the page and use the image for what only an image can show.
Use only images you have the right to use. Pictures found online are usually copyrighted. Use your own, the university’s, or material with a clear licence, and credit the source in the caption.
Never publish anything that identifies a patient unless you hold explicit consent and your institution has approved it. Remember that the finished course will be public (Chapter 8).

title: Images, Tables, Diagrams and References
text:
2 Tables
A table shows a comparison, or a list of items each with the same properties. In Visual mode use Insert → Table and type into the cells. In Source mode a table is drawn with vertical bars:
| Tool | Used for | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| RStudio | Writing and building the course | Free |
| GitHub | Publishing the course | Free for public courses |
: The tools in this course {#tbl-tools}
The line starting with a colon is the caption, and the label works like a figure’s label: @tbl-tools gives Table 2.



Table 2: The tools in this course





Tool
Used for
Cost




RStudio
Writing and building the course
Free


GitHub
Publishing the course
Free for public courses






Keep tables small (rarely more than five columns) and never use a table just to arrange things on the page. If a table gets wide, it usually wants to be two tables, or a list.

title: Images, Tables, Diagrams and References
text:
3 Diagrams without a drawing program
For processes and relationships, you can describe the diagram in text and let the website draw it. This is called Mermaid. It is ideal for flow charts, and diagrams stay editable: to change a box, change a word.
Type a block like this:
```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-flow
%%| fig-cap: "The working rhythm"
%%| fig-alt: "Three boxes in a row: Edit, Render, Check. An arrow leads from each to the next, and from Check back to Edit."
flowchart LR
    A["Edit"] --> B["Render"]
    B --> C["Check"]
    C --> A
```
Each box is letter["Label"], and --> draws an arrow between two of them. The result:






flowchart LR
    A["Edit"] --> B["Render"]
    B --> C["Check"]
    C --> A




Figure 2: The working rhythm





To colour boxes in the university’s palette, add these lines at the end of the diagram and list the boxes that should get each style:
    classDef dark fill:#203151,stroke:#203151,color:#ffffff
    classDef gold fill:#f1a400,stroke:#f1a400,color:#000000
    class A,B dark
    class C gold
The first two lines define a style (dark blue with white text; yellow with black text, as the corporate design allows), the last two apply them. The landing page of this course uses exactly this.






When not to use a diagram



If you find yourself fighting the tool to get a complicated picture, draw it in any program you like, export it as PNG or SVG, and use it as an ordinary image. Do not spend an afternoon on a diagram.

title: Images, Tables, Diagrams and References
text:
4 Video
A short video can explain a movement or a screen recording better than a page of text. Use the video shortcode with a web address or a local file:
{{< video media/hand-disinfection.mp4 >}}
Two things to consider before you add one:

Where it is hosted matters. Embedding a video from a public platform makes the learner’s browser contact that company, which raises data-protection questions for a public university. Prefer a video hosted by the university or your own project, and ask your data-protection officer what is approved.
Provide a transcript or captions. Learners who cannot hear, and learners in a quiet library, need them.

title: Images, Tables, Diagrams and References
text:
5 Citing sources
If you refer to research or guidelines, cite them properly. The template builds the reference list automatically.

Keep your sources in one file, references.bib. Each source has a short key of your choosing, for example roediger2006test.
Cite in the text by typing @ and the key: [@roediger2006test] gives (Roediger and Karpicke 2006). To cite two, separate with a semicolon: [@sweller1988cognitive; @mayer2009multimedia].
The list appears wherever the page references.qmd says so. You do not type it.

You almost never have to write references.bib by hand. If you use the reference manager Zotero, export your collection as BibTeX and save it over references.bib. In RStudio’s Visual mode, Insert → Citation… can also look a source up by its DOI and add it for you.






Cite for the learner, not for show



A good course cites where a claim needs support or where a learner might want to read further. It does not need a citation after every sentence. Two or three well-chosen sources per chapter are plenty.

title: Images, Tables, Diagrams and References
text:
6 Check your understanding




Where should the image files for the course be stored?

Anywhere; the website finds them
In the images/ folder of the project
In the docs/ folder
Pasted into a Word document next to the chapter


Keep all pictures in images/, so they are in one place and the links in your chapters stay short and consistent. Never place anything in docs/; it is overwritten at every render.



Which is the best alt text for a screenshot of the Build tab?

Screenshot
image1.png
The Build tab in RStudio, with the Render Website button highlighted
Look at the picture above


Alt text should say what the picture shows and why it is there, so that someone who cannot see it gets the same information.



You have a 6 MB photograph from a phone camera. What should you do before using it?

Nothing; the website compresses it automatically
Scale it down to about 1600 pixels wide and save it as a JPG
Convert it to a table
Type the caption into the picture


The website serves the file exactly as it is, so a huge image slows every learner’s page down. Scale it before you add it.


In the text, a citation is written by typing the sign ? followed by the key.

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
In this chapter

Write learning objectives that say what a learner can do
Cut a topic into chapters of a sensible size
Find the four places that make up the project’s skeleton
Add, reorder and remove chapters
Start your own course from the empty chapter skeleton

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
1 Plan on paper first
The most common mistake in online courses is starting with the material: “I have forty slides, let me put them online.” Start with the learner instead. Three questions, in this order:

Who is it for, and what do they already know?
What should they be able to do afterwards? Not “know about” or “understand”, but do.
How will they, and you, find out that they can?

Only then decide what to teach. Planning backwards from the outcome like this is sometimes called backward design (Wiggins and McTighe 2005), and it removes most of the material you would otherwise have felt obliged to include.

Writing objectives that can be checked
An objective is useful when you can imagine the question that tests it. Vague verbs cannot be tested; concrete verbs can (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001).



Table 1: Turning vague objectives into checkable ones









Vague
Concrete




Understand hand hygiene
List the five moments for hand disinfection


Know the consent process
Explain to a patient, in plain words, what they are consenting to


Be familiar with the system
Enter a new patient record without help






Aim for three to six objectives per course and two to four per chapter. They go at the top of the page in the blue objectives panel, and they become your quiz questions later.


Cut it into chapters
A chapter should be one topic that a learner can finish in a single sitting, roughly 15 to 30 minutes. This is a rule of thumb, not a law, but there is good reason behind it: people can hold only a few new things in mind at once, so material that introduces one idea at a time, and lets the learner use it before adding the next, is easier to learn from (Sweller 1988).
Inside a chapter, follow the same rhythm every time. Learners then always know where they are:

Objectives (what this chapter is for)
Explanation in short sections, each with its own heading
A key point box for the one thing to remember
Questions to check understanding

That last step is not decoration. Answering a question about something you just read helps you remember it far better than reading it again (Roediger and Karpicke 2006). Put the questions in.






Use the worksheet



Before creating any file, fill in this table on paper. If you cannot complete a row, that is the part of the course to think about next.









Chapter title
Objective (what can the learner do?)
How will they check it?
Length

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
2 The four places that matter
Everything in the project is either a chapter, a setting, a picture or the appearance. You only need to know four places:



Table 2: The project skeleton










Where
What it holds
You edit it




01-….qmd, 02-….qmd, …
The chapters, one file each
Constantly


_quarto.yml
The settings: course title, chapter order, footer
When you add or reorder chapters, and once at the start


images/
Pictures, and the logo
When you add pictures


assets/
Colours, fonts and quiz behaviour, already set up in the university’s corporate design
Never, unless you are asked to






Besides these: index.qmd is the landing page, glossary.qmd and references.qmd are the reference pages, slides/ holds lecture slides, and docs/ is where the finished website appears. Do not edit anything in docs/.

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
3 Name your files
Chapter files are named with a number, then a short description: 03-write-text.qmd. The rules are boring but they prevent trouble:

Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only. No spaces, no umlauts.
The number keeps them in order in the Files panel. It does not control the order on the website; the settings file does.
A file whose name starts with an underscore, like _draft-chapter.qmd, is ignored when the website is built. Use that for unfinished work.

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
4 The chapter list: _quarto.yml
Open _quarto.yml. Most of the file you can leave alone. The part that matters for structure is the sidebar: block, which is the chapter list learners see on the left of every page:
  sidebar:
    style: docked
    contents:
      - index.qmd
      - section: "Basics"
        contents:
          - 01-first-steps.qmd
          - 02-the-workflow.qmd
      - section: "Practice"
        contents:
          - 03-exercises.qmd
Read it top to bottom and it matches the sidebar exactly: a landing page, then a group called Basics with two chapters, then a group called Practice with one.






This file is strict about spaces



Indentation carries meaning here. Use spaces, never the Tab key. Each level is indented two spaces further, a dash is followed by a space, and a colon is followed by a space. When in doubt, copy an existing line and change only the words.



Add a chapter

Copy _chapter-skeleton.qmd, and name the copy, say, 04-feedback.qmd.
Open it, change the title: at the top and write the chapter.
In _quarto.yml, add one line in the right place in the list: - 04-feedback.qmd, indented to match its neighbours.
Render.



Reorder, group or remove

Reorder: move the line up or down in the list.
Group: put chapters under a - section: "Name" block, as above.
Remove: delete its line from the list, then delete the file (or put an underscore in front of its name to keep it as a draft). If you delete the file but leave the line, the render will complain that it cannot find it.

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
5 The top menu
The bar across the top has a few links (Course, Slides, Glossary). They are listed under navbar: in the same file, in the same style. Keep it short: three or four links. The chapters belong in the sidebar, not here.

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
6 Start your own course
You have two sensible ways to begin.

Keep this course as your manualStart from an empty project


Make a copy of the whole project folder for your own course, and keep the original untouched. Then you can consult this course while you work on yours. This is what we recommend for a first course.



Copy the project folder and rename it as in Chapter 1.
In _quarto.yml, replace the chapter list with your own (start with just index.qmd and one chapter).
Delete the eight chapter files of this course, or put an underscore in front of them to keep them out of the build.
Create your first chapter from _chapter-skeleton.qmd.
Edit index.qmd for your own course, and change the title, description and footer in _quarto.yml.

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
7 The landing page
index.qmd is the first thing a learner sees. It should answer five questions in a few lines each: What is this course? Who is it for? What will I be able to do afterwards? How long does it take? What do I need beforehand? Put the objectives panel and a short route through the chapters on it. This course’s own landing page is a working example.

title: Plan and Structure Your Course
text:
8 Check your understanding




Which of these is a learning objective that can be checked?

Understand the principles of good communication
Be aware of the risks of the procedure
Explain the three main risks of the procedure to a colleague
Appreciate the importance of documentation


Only the third names something a learner does that you could ask a question about. “Understand”, “be aware of” and “appreciate” describe an inner state you cannot observe.



You rename 05-quality.qmd to _05-quality.qmd. What happens at the next render?

It appears at the top of the sidebar
It is skipped, so it is not built into the website
The render fails
It is published with a “draft” label


A leading underscore tells the build to ignore a file. It is the simplest way to keep unfinished work in the project without publishing it. If the chapter is still listed in _quarto.yml, remove that line too.



The order of chapters in the sidebar is decided by:

The numbers in the file names
The alphabetical order of the titles
The order of the lines in _quarto.yml
The date the files were last edited


File numbers only help you keep the Files panel tidy. The sidebar follows the list in the settings file, so reordering means moving a line.


A chapter should take a learner roughly ? minutes. (Type a number of minutes and click elsewhere; anything from 10 to 30 counts.)

title: Set Up and First Render
text:
In this chapter

Explain in one sentence how text files become a course website
Install R and RStudio
Open the project and build the website for the first time
Make one change and see it appear

title: Set Up and First Render
text:
1 The idea in three sentences
You write your course as ordinary text files, one per chapter. You press one button, and the software turns those files into a finished website: navigation, search, quizzes, the university’s colours and logo, all included. That website is just a folder of files, which you then put on GitHub or GitLab, where it is shown to learners as a normal web address.
Think of it like exporting a Word document to PDF. You write, you press export, you get the finished thing. The difference is that the “finished thing” is a whole website, and that this one already looks the way the university expects.

Key point
You never edit the website itself. You edit the text files and render (build) the website again. If something on the website is wrong, you fix the text file, not the web page.

title: Set Up and First Render
text:
2 Step 1: install R and RStudio
Two free programs, installed in this order.

R — the engine underneath. Download from cran.r-project.org: choose your operating system, then the download link for the latest version, and run the installer with the default choices.
RStudio Desktop — the program you actually work in. Download from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop and install it.

RStudio includes Quarto, the tool that builds the website. There is nothing else to install.






You will not write R code



This template contains no R code, and you do not need to know any. R is only the engine that RStudio runs on. You will work with text, images and quiz questions.








On a managed work computer



If you are not allowed to install programs, ask your IT support for R and RStudio Desktop. Many institutions offer them through a software portal. Tell them you need RStudio Desktop with Quarto, so they install a version recent enough to include it.

title: Set Up and First Render
section: 3 Step 2: put the project in the right place
text:
3 Step 2: put the project in the right place
You receive the template as a folder (or a zip file, which you unzip first).

Copy the folder to a normal location on your own computer, such as Documents.
Rename it to something that describes your course, for example wound-care-course. Use lowercase letters and hyphens; avoid spaces, umlauts and special characters.
Inside, rename course-template.Rproj to the same name, for example wound-care-course.Rproj.







Avoid synchronised and network folders



Keep the project on the computer’s own disk. Folders that are continuously synchronised (cloud storage) or that live on a network drive can be slow and can lock files while the website is being built, which causes confusing errors.

title: Set Up and First Render
section: 4 Step 3: open the project and build the website
text:
4 Step 3: open the project and build the website

Double-click the .Rproj file. RStudio opens with the project loaded.
Find the Build tab, usually in the upper-right panel.
Click Render Website.

The first build takes a minute or two. Progress appears in a panel labelled Background Jobs, and when it finishes, the website opens in RStudio’s Viewer pane or in your browser. That is your course, running.






If there is no Build tab



RStudio only shows it when the project was opened through the .Rproj file. Use File → Open Project… and choose that file.


The finished website is written to a folder called docs inside your project. Chapter 8 explains why it has that name and what to do with it. For now, just know that this folder is the product: everything a learner sees is in there.

title: Set Up and First Render
text:
5 Step 4: your first edit

In RStudio’s Files panel, click index.qmd to open it.
Change the title: line at the top to something of your own.
Save (Ctrl+S, or Cmd+S on a Mac).
Click Render Website again.

Your new title appears. That is the whole working rhythm of this course: edit, save, render, look. Repeat as often as you like; nothing you do can break the original, and a render is harmless.

Editing without seeing the markup
The file you just opened shows some symbols (#, *, :::). That is the source view. You do not have to live there. At the top-left of the editor there are two buttons, Source and Visual. Click Visual and the file looks like a word processor: bold and italic buttons, bullet lists, an Insert menu for pictures, tables and callouts. The text underneath is written for you.
Most authors work in Visual mode and switch to Source only to fix something particular. Chapters 3 and 4 show both views side by side.

title: Set Up and First Render
text:
6 What if something goes wrong?



Table 1: Common first-day problems










What you see
What it usually means
What to do




An error message in the Background Jobs panel
A typo in a text file. The message names the file and often the line
Open that file, look at the line named, compare with a working example


The error mentions the settings file, _quarto.yml
Wrong indentation. That file is fussy about spaces
Use spaces, never the Tab key; copy an existing block and change only the words


The page still shows old content
It was not rebuilt
Click Render Website again and refresh the browser (Ctrl+F5)


Search does not work when you double-click a page in docs
Search needs the site to be served, not opened from disk
Use the preview RStudio gives you after rendering, or check search once the site is published

title: Set Up and First Render
text:
7 Check your understanding




You spot a spelling mistake on a page of the finished website. Where do you fix it?

In the HTML file inside the docs folder
In the .qmd text file, then render the website again
In the browser, by clicking on the text
In the .Rproj file


The website is generated from the text files. If you correct the generated file, your fix is overwritten the next time you render. Always correct the source.



Do you need to know how to program in R to use this template?

Yes, at least the basics
No. R is only the engine RStudio runs on; you work with text and menus
Yes, but only to build the quizzes
Only if the course has images


The template contains no R code. Quizzes are written as plain text, and images and tables are inserted from menus or with a few characters of markup.


The working rhythm of this course is: edit, save, ?, look. (Type the missing word and click elsewhere. Render is the word for building the website from the text files; in RStudio it is the Render Website button.)

title: Write Text
text:
In this chapter

Write and format text in Visual mode, and read the same text in Source mode
Structure a page with headings that work for navigation and screen readers
Use callouts, tabs, key-point boxes and footnotes in the right places
Link to other chapters and to the glossary

title: Write Text
section: 1 Two views of the same file
text:
1 Two views of the same file
Every chapter is a text file. RStudio shows it in one of two ways, switched by the Source and Visual buttons at the top-left of the editor.

Visual looks like a word processor. Use the toolbar for bold, lists and links, and the Insert menu for pictures, tables, callouts and more.
Source shows the plain text, with a few symbols marking the formatting. This is called markdown.

You can switch at any time without losing anything. If you never want to see markdown, you never have to. But it is worth being able to read it, because this course shows examples in that form, and because a fix in Source view is sometimes faster than hunting for the right menu.

title: Write Text
text:
2 Markdown in one table
The left column is what you type in Source view. The right column is what the reader sees.



Table 1: The handful of markdown symbols you will use daily





You type
The reader sees




## A heading
(a section heading, see below)


**important**
important


*emphasis*
emphasis


`file.qmd`
file.qmd


- item on a new line
a bullet point


1. step on a new line
a numbered step


[the glossary](glossary.qmd)
the glossary


> quotation
a quotation block






A blank line separates paragraphs. A list needs a blank line before it. That is nearly all there is.

title: Write Text
text:
3 The top of every file
Each chapter starts with a small block between two lines of three dashes:
---
title: "Write Text"
subtitle: "Headings, emphasis, links, and the boxes that make a page easy to read"
---
The title becomes the page heading and the entry in the sidebar. The subtitle is optional and appears underneath. Keep the quotation marks and the dashes.

title: Write Text
text:
4 Headings
Use headings to divide the chapter into short sections. In Source view they are lines starting with ## (a main section) or ### (a subsection):
## Main section

### A subsection inside it
In Visual mode, use the paragraph-style drop-down in the toolbar and choose Heading 2 or Heading 3.
Three rules, because headings do more work than they appear to:

Do not use # (a single hash) inside a chapter. The page title already uses that level. Start with ##.
Never skip a level. A ### belongs under a ##.
Never fake a heading with bold text. Real headings feed the “On this page” list on the right, the automatic numbering, and search. They are also how people using a screen reader jump around the page. Bold text does none of that.


Key point
A learner scans before they read. Make the headings tell the story on their own: “How to add a chapter” beats “Chapters”.

title: Write Text
text:
5 Writing for the screen
Reading on a screen is not reading on paper. A few habits help:

Short paragraphs, three or four sentences.
Say the point first, then explain.
Link text should make sense alone. “Read the glossary” is good; “click here” is not, because screen-reader users often hear a list of links with no surrounding text.
Use lists when items are parallel, and numbered lists only when order matters.
Write in the second person (“you will”) and keep sentences plain.

title: Write Text
text:
6 Linking
To link to another chapter, use its file name, not a web address:
See [Chapter 2](02-plan-and-structure.qmd) for how to add a chapter.
This keeps working after the course is published, even if the web address changes. To link to another website, use the full address starting with https://. In Visual mode, select the words and press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on a Mac).

title: Write Text
text:
7 Boxes that carry meaning
Boxes draw the eye, so each kind should mean one thing, and a page should have few of them. This template has two families.

Callouts
Callouts are built in. There are five kinds; the colour and icon follow the university’s palette.






Note



Extra information that is useful but not essential.








Tip



A shortcut or a piece of good practice.








Important



Something the reader must not miss.








Warning



A step where mistakes are likely or costly.








Caution



Something that can cause a problem in specific circumstances.


In Source view a callout is written like this. The words after callout- pick the kind, and the ## line is its title:
::: {.callout-warning}
## Warning

A step where mistakes are likely or costly.
:::
In Visual mode, use Insert → Callout. Add collapse="true" inside the braces to make a callout start folded, which is useful for extra detail:






Click to unfold: an optional detail





Folded callouts keep the main path short. Learners who want the detail can open it; the rest can skip it.





Objectives and key point
Two boxes are specific to this template. Both are made the same way, with a ::: {.name} line, their content, and a closing :::. In Visual mode use Insert → Div… and type the class name (objectives or keypoint) into the attributes field.

ObjectivesKey point


Once, at the top of a chapter, in blue.
::: {.objectives}
**In this chapter**

- Write objectives that can be checked
- Cut a topic into chapters
:::


Once per section at most, in yellow. The one thing to remember.
::: {.keypoint}
**Key point**

You edit the text files, never the finished website.
:::



Tabs, as you just used, are also useful for alternatives such as “Windows” and “Mac”. Each ## heading inside a ::: {.panel-tabset} block becomes a tab.

title: Write Text
text:
Footnotes


Like this one. It appears at the bottom of the page, and pops up when you hover over the number.↩︎

title: Write Text
text:
9 Explaining terms
Every field has words that learners do not know yet. Put them in the glossary page (glossary.qmd), and mark the first use in the text so that hovering shows the meaning. For example, the word render below has a dotted underline: on a computer, hover to see the explanation.
Click [render]{.gloss title="Build the website from the text files"} again.
Hover text does not appear on touch screens, so the glossary page is the primary place for definitions. The hover is a convenience.

title: Write Text
text:
10 Check your understanding




You want to start a new section in the middle of a chapter. What do you type?

# New section
## New section
**New section**
NEW SECTION


## makes a real heading, one level below the page title. A single # is reserved for the title, and bold text is not a heading at all, so it would not appear in the “On this page” list.



Which link text is best?

Click here for the glossary
https://…/glossary.html
Look up the term in the glossary
Link


Good link text describes the destination and makes sense when read on its own, which is how screen-reader users often meet links.



For a warning that only some readers need to see, in full detail, you should use:

A key-point box
A callout with collapse="true"
A heading
Red text


A folded callout keeps the main text short and leaves the detail to whoever wants it. Red text is not part of the template’s palette, and colour alone should never carry the meaning anyway.


The symbol pair you type around a word to make it bold is two ?. (Type the word, or the symbol.)

title: Quizzes
text:
In this chapter

Write a multiple-choice question with feedback
Write a fill-in-the-blank question for a word or a number
Add a running score to a page
Write questions that teach, not just test
State what these quizzes can and cannot do

title: Quizzes
section: 1 Why quizzes belong in every chapter
text:
1 Why quizzes belong in every chapter
Answering a question about something you have just read is one of the most reliable ways to remember it. In the classic experiments, learners who were tested on a passage remembered more a week later than learners who simply read it again (Roediger and Karpicke 2006). So the questions at the end of a chapter are not an extra: they are part of the teaching.
The template has a small quiz tool built in. You write questions as plain text, and the website turns them into clickable questions. Nothing needs installing, and nothing is sent anywhere.

title: Quizzes
text:
2 Multiple choice
A question is a block that starts with ::: {.question} and ends with :::. Inside: the question, a list of options, and (optionally) an explanation. Mark the correct option with an x between the brackets.
::: {.question}
Which file holds the chapter order?

- [ ] index.qmd
- [x] _quarto.yml
- [ ] references.bib

::: {.feedback}
The list under `sidebar:` in `_quarto.yml` decides the order.
:::
:::
Here is the result. Try it, and try getting it wrong to see what happens.

Which file holds the chapter order?

index.qmd
_quarto.yml
references.bib


The list under sidebar: in _quarto.yml decides the order.


The learner picks an option and presses Check answer. The right option turns blue with a tick; a wrong choice turns yellow with a cross; and the explanation appears either way. Options are locked afterwards, so the learner cannot simply click through them all.
Exactly one option must be marked correct. Everything between the options and the ::: {.feedback} block is optional, but the feedback is where the teaching happens, so please always write it.
In Visual mode, the easiest way is to write the question as an ordinary paragraph, type the options as a task list (Insert → Task List or a bullet list with checkboxes), and wrap the whole thing with Insert → Div…, class question. Many authors find it quicker to copy a finished question in Source view and change the words.

title: Quizzes
text:
3 Fill in the blank
For a word, name or number that the learner should recall, put a marker right in the sentence:
The tool that builds the website is called [?]{.fitb answer="Quarto"}.
The tool that builds the website is called ?. Try typing it, then click elsewhere.
The [?] becomes a small input box. Some details:

Case and spaces do not matter: “quarto” is accepted.
Several accepted answers: separate them with a vertical bar, for example answer="qmd|.qmd".
Numbers are graded as numbers. Add a tolerance with tol: [?]{.fitb answer="20" tol="10"} accepts anything from 10 to 30. Without tol, the number must match to within 0.01. A decimal comma is accepted as well as a decimal point.







Do not wrap a fill-in in a question block



A fill-in is a sentence with a blank. Put it straight into the running text, as above. The ::: {.question} block is only for multiple choice.

title: Quizzes
text:
4 A running score
To show a scoreboard that counts correct answers on the page, place an empty block above your questions:
::: {.quiz-score}
:::
It shows “0 / 3” and updates as the learner answers. It counts the multiple-choice questions on that page. Every chapter in this course has one.

title: Quizzes
text:
5 Writing questions that teach
A question is only as good as its wrong answers and its feedback.

Test the objective, not trivia. Look at the objective for the chapter and write a question that checks exactly that.
Make the wrong options plausible. Each should be something a learner who has misunderstood would actually choose. Silly options teach nothing.
Avoid “all of the above” and “none of the above”. They reward guessing strategy rather than knowledge.
Keep options similar in length and put the correct one in a varying position. The template does not shuffle the options, so vary them yourself.
Explain in the feedback. Say why the right answer is right and, briefly, why the tempting wrong one is not. Feedback on a wrong answer is where most of the learning occurs.
Two to four questions per chapter is usually enough.


Key point
Write the feedback first. If you cannot explain why an answer is right in two sentences, the question is not ready.

title: Quizzes
section: 6 What these quizzes are, and are not
text:
6 What these quizzes are, and are not






Self-check, not an examination



The answers are checked inside the learner’s own browser. Nothing is recorded, no score is sent to you, and there is no login. A learner who looks at the page source can read the right answers.
That makes these quizzes ideal for practice and immediate feedback, and unsuitable for anything that counts towards a grade, a certificate or a licence. For those, use the test tools of your learning platform, and link to your course from there.


If you need to know how learners are doing, the honest options are a short survey at the end, or a linked exercise in your learning platform.

title: Quizzes
text:
7 Check your understanding




How do you mark the correct option in a multiple-choice question?

Write the word “correct” after it
Put an x in its brackets: - [x] option
Make it bold
Put it first in the list


The x in the brackets marks the correct option. Position and formatting make no difference, so put the right answer wherever suits the question.



A colleague wants to use these quizzes for the final exam of a course, with results sent to the teacher. What is your advice?

Go ahead; the score is saved automatically
Add a name field to every question
Use the platform’s test tool instead; these quizzes record nothing and the answers can be read in the page source
Hide the answers in white text


The quizzes run entirely in the reader’s browser, by design. They are excellent for practice and useless for assessment. Hiding the answers in white text would not hide them from anyone who knows to look, and it would break accessibility.



What is the most useful part of a question for learning?

The number of options
The score counter
The feedback that explains why an answer is right or wrong
The colour of the correct option


The moment after a learner answers is the moment they most want to know why. Use it.


In a multiple-choice question, the correct option is the one with the letter ? between its brackets.

title: Check Before Release
text:
In this chapter

Find leftover template text and placeholder settings
Review a course for accessibility in ten minutes
Test the course on a small screen and in dark mode
Recognise the legal and privacy questions to settle before going public
Get one other person to test it
Once a course is public, learners will find every typo, broken link and leftover “Placeholder” for you. A structured check before release costs an hour and saves the awkward emails. Work through the sections below in order.

title: Check Before Release
text:
1 1. Content

Every chapter has objectives at the top, and every objective is covered by at least one question.
Read each chapter once, aloud or slowly. You will hear what you cannot see: sentences that are too long, steps out of order.
Run the spell checker. In RStudio, open a chapter and press F7 (or use Edit → Check Spelling). Do it for every file.
Check facts, numbers and dates, especially anything that might have changed since you wrote it.
Click every link to an outside website. Web addresses go out of date.

title: Check Before Release
text:
2 2. Leftover template text
The commonest slip is publishing the template’s own words. Use RStudio’s search across all files: Edit → Find in Files… (Ctrl+Shift+F, or Cmd+Shift+F on a Mac). Search for each of these, and fix every hit outside the parts of the course that you deliberately kept:

Course Template
example.org
Placeholder
Your name
placeholder.svg

Then open _quarto.yml and check the lines marked CHANGE: the course title, the description, the web address (site-url), the chapter list and the footer. Also check index.qmd: the author line and the date.

title: Check Before Release
text:
3 3. The look
Render the whole website with Render Website, not just a single file, so no stale pages remain. Then look at it the way learners will:

On a small screen. Make the browser window narrow (drag its edge) until the layout switches to the phone view. Text should stay readable, and no horizontal scrolling should be needed. Better still, open the published site on a real phone once.
In dark mode. Switch your computer to dark appearance and reload. Text, boxes and the logo should stay legible.
In the print preview, if learners will print chapters.
In the search. Type a word you know is in a chapter, and confirm it is found. Search works on the published site, and may not when you open the files from disk.

title: Check Before Release
text:
4 4. Accessibility
A course that not everyone can use is unfinished. Ten minutes:

Alt text on every image (Chapter 4). No “image1”.
Headings in order, never skipped, never faked with bold text (Chapter 3).
Link text that makes sense alone. Search your chapters for “click here”.
No information by colour alone. If a sentence says “the red button”, add a name.
Video has captions or a transcript.
Try the keyboard. Press Tab repeatedly through a page and check that you can reach and use links, menus and the quiz buttons without a mouse.

The standard behind these points is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (World Wide Web Consortium 2023); the template’s colours already pass its contrast requirements, so you only need to keep to the habits above.

title: Check Before Release
text:
5 5. Legal and privacy






Ask, do not guess



The rules for what a public university website must contain, and what may be published, are set by your institution. Confirm the following with the responsible office before release.



Imprint and privacy notice. Public websites in Germany normally need an imprint (Impressum) and, where personal data is processed, a privacy notice. Ask your communications or data-protection office for the standard wording and the address to link to. The footer in _quarto.yml has a commented-out example showing where such a link goes.
Picture, text and video rights. Do you have the right to publish every image, table and quotation? Is each one credited as its licence requires?
Patient and personal data. Nothing that identifies a patient or a colleague, in text, images, screenshots or file names. Look at screenshots for name fields, record numbers and dates of birth.
Third-party services. If you have embedded a video or map from an outside provider, your data-protection office needs to have approved it.
The licence of your own material. State how others may reuse the course, if at all, in the footer or on the landing page.

title: Check Before Release
text:
6 6. A fresh pair of eyes
Ask one person who does not know the subject to work through one chapter while you watch, and say nothing. Note every place they hesitate, re-read or click the wrong thing. These are the places to improve. You will learn more in twenty minutes than in a day of rereading your own text.

title: Check Before Release
text:
7 7. Before you press publish

The whole website has been rendered again after your last change.
Nothing is left in the sidebar that you do not want learners to see. Drafts start with an underscore.
You know what web address the course will have, and it is entered as site-url.

You are ready for Chapter 8.

title: Check Before Release
text:
8 Check your understanding




Which of these is the best way to find leftover placeholder text across the whole project?

Read every chapter again
Use Edit → Find in Files and search for the placeholder words
Ask a learner to report them
Render the website and look at the sidebar


A search across all files finds every hit in seconds, including ones in files you have not opened for weeks. Reading is slower and easily misses things.



A screenshot in your chapter shows the RStudio window on your own computer, including a project name and your user name. What should you do?

Nothing; a screenshot is not personal data
Check it for anything that identifies a person or a patient, and crop or redo it if necessary
Add alt text and move on
Reduce its size


Screenshots regularly reveal names, file paths and records that their authors did not notice. Look at the whole picture, at full size, before publishing.



Why render the whole website before release, rather than only the chapter you last changed?

It is faster
Single pages cannot be published
A full render rebuilds every page and clears out pages that no longer belong to the course
It creates the search box


A full render leaves the output folder in the exact state that will be published, with no stale leftovers from earlier versions.


The menu you use in RStudio to search through every file at once is called Edit → Find in ?.

title: References and Further Reading
text:
The learning-design advice in this course rests on a small number of well-known sources: planning from the outcome backwards (Wiggins and McTighe 2005), writing objectives with concrete verbs (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001), limiting how much is new at once (Sweller 1988), combining words with pictures (Mayer 2009), and using questions to help learners remember (Roediger and Karpicke 2006). The accessibility habits follow the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (World Wide Web Consortium 2023).
